Madam Justice J. Mackinnon

Introduction

[
1
]

Olivia Greenberg was born on December 21, 1998.
Her parents separated on August 17, 2002.  Litigation between them commenced in
November of that year.  Custody and access were primary issues.  The case
continued in court until a consent final Order was obtained on July 22, 2005.
That Order provided for joint custody, with equal sharing of holidays, and with
Olivia to reside during the school year with her father from Thursday after
school until Monday morning in one week and from Thursday after school until
Friday morning in the next week, alternating, and for the balance of time, with
her mother.  This arrangement provided for an approximate 60:40 division of
residential time as between the mother and father respectively.  The Order was
very detailed, containing 67 paragraphs related to Olivia’s custody and access.

[
2
]

In March and April 2007 both the mother and father
filed applications in court to change the terms of the July 22, 2005 Order.
After five case conferences, one motion and two unsuccessful settlement
conferences the case came to trial.  Including this current trial, the
Greenbergs have now come to court on 23 occasions, appearing before 13
different judges and masters.  The trial itself extended over 16 days.

[
3
]

The claims at trial were these:

By the Applicant

1.         An
order of sole custody and final decision making with respect to major issues,
activities and scheduling disputes pertaining to Olivia.

2.         No
changes to the current residential schedule, primary residence of Olivia to the
Applicant.

3.         Child
support and s. 7 expenses in proportion to the parents’ incomes, retroactive to
July 2005, including income imputation to the Respondent.

4.         Costs.

By the
Respondent

1.         Joint custody and equal residential time for Olivia with
each parent.

2.         Primary
residence of Olivia, for school boundary purposes, to the Respondent.

3.         Child
support retroactive to July 2005 calculated by the shared custody method and
s.7 expenses in proportion to the parents’ incomes.

4.         An
order for a stipulated protocol for Olivia’s asthma care.

5.         A
decision as to how the regular weekend access rotation will recommence after
holidays.

6.         Costs.

[
4
]

In short form, the mother’s position at trial
was that the joint custody order had proven unworkable by reason of the high
conflict between the parents, for which she asserted that the father was mainly
responsible.  In her submission granting her sole decision making in major
categories would significantly reduce the conflict and this would greatly
benefit Olivia.  She did not seek to reduce the father’s time with Olivia, but
would accept the court’s decision in that respect.  She submitted that the
father was underemployed, that he should be deemed to have an income of $60,000
per year and should pay child support and his share of special expenses on that
basis.

[
5
]

In short form, the father’s position was that
the parents had a demonstrated track record of effective co-parenting such that
joint custody should be continued.  In his submission Olivia should reside with
each parent in alternating one week periods throughout the year.  He asserted
that this was what he had always wanted, Olivia preferred it as well, and it
would be best for her to spend equal time with each parent.

[
6
]

In terms of child support, the father wished to
change the July 2005 Order retroactively to reduce his child support payments
to the set-off amount only.  He maintained that his income should be accepted
as $30,000 per year, primarily because he was self-represented and had to
devote so much time to this court case.

[
7
]

The mother maintains that the fact that joint
decision making is unworkable, combined with the stress of the conflict upon
Olivia constitutes a material change in circumstances.  The father maintains
that his remarriage in 2007 and the presence of his wife’s daughter Sarah who
is one year apart from Olivia constitute a material change in circumstances.
He also relies on Olivia’s wishes in this regard.  Both parents submitted that
the other had failed to prove the necessary material change in circumstances.
That is, the father submitted that the mother had not made out a material
change of circumstances to warrant a change to the existing joint custody, and
the mother submitted that the father had not made out a material change of
circumstances to warrant a change to the existing residential arrangements.

Overview

[
8
]

The final Order dated July 22, 2005 provides
that the parents shall have joint custody of Olivia, so that each will have an
equal role and say in significant decisions for Olivia, with the exception that
the mother shall have decision making for all routine medical matters and the
father shall have decision making authority for all routine dental matters.
The agreement also provided that as co-parents the parties would make important
decisions about Olivia’s welfare together, in good faith, and in Olivia’s best
interests, including decisions regarding the following:

(a)

Education;

(b)

Major, non-emergency health care;

(c)

Major recreational activities; and

(d)

Religious activities.

[
9
]

The parties were to communicate via e-mail and
to confine their e-mail to the exchange of information about Olivia in a child
focused and positive way.  Other specific provisions dealt with holidays,
Mother’s and Father’s Day, long weekends, special occasions, travel, schooling,
extracurricular activities, supporting the parent/child relationship, and
conflict resolution.

[
10
]

The parents have always agreed that Olivia will
be raised in the Jewish faith.  They have agreed, since grade one, that she
will attend Hillel Academy to the conclusion of grade 8.  This is a Jewish
parochial private school paid for equally by Olivia’s two sets of
grandparents.  The parents have also been able to communicate information to
each other via e-mail, such as related to school activities, forgotten items,
pick up times, birthday parties and play dates for Olivia, and routine
healthcare matters.  Hundreds of e-mails and other written communications
between the parties were tendered at trial.  They do show information sharing
between the parents, but little if any decision making about contentious
issues, including interpretation of the final Order.

[
11
]

The exhibits and oral testimony of the parents
reveal significant contention between them in numerous categories.  These
include:

•

Treatment of Olivia’s asthma

•

Provision of counselling for Olivia

•

School issues: tutoring, after school care,
uniforms, high school

•

Extracurricular activities

•

Holidays

•

Resumption of the weekend rotation after
holidays

•

Mother’s day

•

Summer camp

[
12
]

They also reveal real difficulty in areas where
flexibility is required or requested.  Serious acrimony has arisen to Olivia’s
detriment when the parents are in each other’s and Olivia’s presence at the
same time and place.  Third parties who are involved in one way or another with
Olivia have been brought into the conflict.  A number of the good faith
provisions in the final Order have been breached.  Olivia has been involved in
the conflict and impacted by it.  In particular, many of the father’s e-mails
reveal clearly that he has engaged Olivia in discussions about issues between
the parents, involved her in their conflict, and influenced her against her
mother.

[
13
]

A psychological assessment was ordered by the
court.  It was conducted by Dr. Alex Weinberger.  He concluded that the
“plethora of documents available for review reflects enough conflict [that] it
overrides what cooperative effort exists.”  He agreed that this was a “high
conflict” case and that Olivia had been influenced to some extent by her father
in voicing her preference for equal residential time with him.  Despite these
conclusions he stated that conflict in and of itself is not the deciding
factor, rather it is a child’s needs and best interests.  He recommended joint
custody with equal residential time on an alternating weekly basis, a mandatory
arbitration clause to resolve disputes, and counselling for each family member.

[
14
]

Interestingly, the mother agrees with and
supports Dr. Weinberger’s observations and findings as set out in the body of
his report.  She disagrees with his recommendations.  The father agrees with
Dr. Weinberger’s recommendations, yet disagrees with many of his findings and
observations.

[
15
]

My conclusion is that the mother has established
a material change in circumstances warranting a change from joint custody to
sole custody so that she will be the parent responsible for Olivia’s major
decisions.  The parents’ track record is not one of effective decision making
and communication.  Olivia has been exposed to and negatively impacted by their
conflict.  In particular, the father’s extremely harsh and negative attitude towards
the mother prevents effective co-parenting and is rubbing off on Olivia,
contrary to her best interests.

[
16
]

I have also concluded that the father has not
demonstrated a material change in circumstances in relation to the residential
arrangements for Olivia.  His remarriage and the fact that his wife also has a
daughter to whom Olivia has become close do not meet this threshold test.  Nor
do Olivia’s views, given the influence brought to bear upon her and her age.

[
17
]

In my view, the conflict resolution clause
recommended by Dr. Weinberger will not work to reduce the conflict between the
parents.  There has already been a conflict resolution provision in place since
July 2005, which proved unsuccessful.  The better approach to reduce conflict
in this case, in my view, is to eliminate as many areas of potential
uncertainty and disagreement from the formal structure of the order as
possible.  This will mean that the arrangements for Olivia will need to be
certain and inflexible.  Flexibility and negotiated changes to the routine should
no longer be attempted in the interest of ending the conflict that Olivia has
been exposed to for so many years.

[
18
]

Finally, I was not persuaded that the mother
should have the final say with respect to Olivia’s activities and schedule.  In
my view, that would only serve to prolong and perhaps even to inflame the
conflict.  For this reason I have given strict, inflexible directions as to the
schedule and as to when each parent can enroll her in activities.  It is my
intention that these provisions not be the subject of debate between the
parents, rather set in stone, in order to eliminate areas of potential
dispute.  In some ways, this lack of scope for flexibility is regrettable, but
in the circumstances, this approach is the most likely to succeed in sheltering
Olivia from parental conflict, and for this reason is in her best interests.

Medical Issues

•

Olivia’s Asthma Treatment

[
19
]

Paragraph one of the July 2005 Order provides as follows:

1.         The Applicant (hereafter “Manya”) and
Gary (hereafter “Gary”) shall have joint custody of the child (hereafter “Olivia”)
so that each will have an equal role and say in significant decisions for
Olivia, with the exception that Manya shall have decision making authority for
all routine medical matters and Gary shall have decision making authority for
all routine dental matters.  The parties shall consult with each other and
advise each other of all routine appointments and outcomes from the
medical/dental appointments and the other party shall not attend the routine
medical/dental appointment unless the party having decision making authority
provides consent in writing.  Further, either party shall have the right to
contact the medical/dental specialist to make inquiries as needed.

[
20
]

Pursuant to this paragraph, the mother took care of Olivia’s
appointments with her allergist, Dr. Chad, in relation to asthma.  At one
point, Olivia’s asthma was quite problematic and her mother was concerned that
she was using so much Ventolin, without good results.  On October 19, 2007, she
consulted with Dr. Chad.  He recommended two different medications and directed
that Olivia no longer use Ventolin.  Ms. Greenberg notified Mr. Greenberg right
away.  Immediately he attacked Dr. Chad’s decision and directed Ms. Greenberg
to keep the Ventolin with Olivia.  He called Dr. Chad, following which Ms.
Greenberg was notified that Dr. Chad would no longer keep Olivia as a patient.
Ms. Greenberg was able to persuade Dr. Chad to reconsider.

[
21
]

Dr. Weinberger reported on this as follows:

The parents had signed a consent at my request
to enable [me] to speak with Dr. Chad.  Ms. Greenberg was of the view that Dr.
Chad would speak to his dealings with Mr. Greenberg which were confrontation,
and thereby illustrate how difficult the father can be to deal with.  Mr.
Greenberg signed the consent but noted that he and Dr. Chad had a disagreement
because he had questioned Dr. Chad’s judgment in not prescribing Ventolin as a
back-up medication to the Symbicort for Olivia.  Mr. Greenberg stated that the
interaction had become heated and unpleasant and that he did not appreciate Dr.
Chad’s approach and that he would sue the doctor if his comments proved to be
prejudicial.  Mr. Greenberg’s upsetness with Dr. Chad clearly showed even as he
spoke of his reservation in signing the consent.

Regrettably the consents were subsequently
misplaced.  I did not request a renewal in that I had determined after further
reflection that in that Mr. Greenberg had acknowledged the confrontation it was
not necessary to pursue the matter directly with Dr. Chad.

[
22
]

The e-mail Ms. Greenberg sent to Mr. Greenberg on October 19, 2007 clearly
set out that Olivia was not to take Ventolin or Advair anymore, rather had a
new inhaler with “Symbicort”.  She provided the doctor’s instructions, a
prescription, and noted that she had placed a booklet of instructions on how to
use the medication in Olivia’s bag.

[
23
]

Mr. Greenberg sent Ms. Greenberg six separate responses over the
course of that day.  He told her:

1.         He had
consulted the manufacturer and the website said Symbicort was to be used for 12
years of age and older, whereas Olivia was only 8.  He would be calling Dr.
Chad.

2.         He spoke to
the pharmacist and that Ventolin was still required for emergencies and should
be with Olivia at all times.

3.         He had
spoken to Dr. Chad who confirmed that Symbicort was appropriate for Olivia and
for emergencies.  Nonetheless, Mr. Greenberg still wanted Olivia to have both
drugs with her all the time until he saw that Symbicort worked in an emergency.

4.         He asked
for confirmation that she would keep Ventolin with Olivia and that she would
obtain a second opinion from another allergist.

5.         He told Ms.
Greenberg based on his reading of the Symbicort profile that it may not work
for Olivia in serious acute attacks and he wanted a second opinion.
“Regardless of the second opinion, I will not take any risks with Olivia’s
health as per this FDA report and I would like Olivia to have her Ventolin with
her at ALL times.  Please respect my wishes.”

6.         “Olivia
knows to keep her Ventolin with her at all times if the Symbicort does not work
in an emergency.”

[
24
]

Mr. Greenberg testified that, after a few weeks, he had a comfort
level that the Symbicort was effective and he was happy with it.  He said, “We
agreed on it.”

[
25
]

This is incorrect.  Contrary to the doctor’s clear direction that Olivia
was not to use Ventolin, Mr. Greenberg preferred his own opinion and insisted
on leaving the Ventolin with Olivia and obviously instructed her to use it if
the Symbicort did not work.  Mr. Greenberg maintained this position until at
least November 19 when he sent two further e-mails to Ms. Greenberg in which he
stated:

•

All I want is for Olivia to have her Ventolin as
a “back up” reliever and you and Dr. Chad would rather take risks.

•

I will continue to put the Ventolin in her pouch
and knapsack on my time in the event that the Symbicort does not work in a
major attack.  It is clear you want to take risks with Olivia’s health.

[
26
]

To the contrary, Mr. Greenberg was taking a risk by providing eight
year old Olivia with a drug in contravention of her doctor’s orders and relying
upon her judgment whether to use it or not.  In a letter to the mother’s lawyer
dated June 26, 2008, Mr. Greenberg was still railing against Dr. Chad’s
“decision to remove Olivia’s life saving Ventolin without testing and proving
Symbicort’s effectiveness as a life saving inhaler.”

[
27
]

In fact, the changes made by Dr. Chad to Olivia’s asthma medication
in October 2007 have always proved effective and her asthma has been very well
managed by the two medications then prescribed.

•

Olivia’s Counsellor

[
28
]

On January 24, 2007, Ms. Greenberg wrote to Mr. Greenberg requesting
his consideration to sending Olivia to a child specialist in order to help her
handle her sadness regarding the divorce.  Her mother thought that Olivia had
begun to show anxiety and would benefit from a “neutral corner where she can
express her conflicted feelings.”  Mr. Greenberg’s response was a bombastic
diatribe against the mother.  He refused his consent.  He called her proposal
transparent, ludicrous, and intrusive.  He described Ms. Greenberg as pathetic
and untrustworthy.  He said:

I will not agree to counseling or therapy for
Olivia as you have provided zero evidence she needs it.  Please provide ample
evidence outlining days and times and circumstances where Olivia has had emotional
difficulty maintaining her life.  Please provide evidence where she is not
eating well, she is emotionally unstable, not social with her friends, not
performing well in school, not doing well in her extra curricular, not happy
and etc…

I trust evidence with affidavits, not just what
you say.  If Olivia is having a difficult time while with you, please provide
affidavits from people that have witnessed Olivia display unstable and
depressed behaviour during your access time.  I am very curious to see these
affidavits.

[
29
]

He threatened to “find out from Olivia exactly what the problems
are, if they exist.”  He threatened, if the mother pursued counselling for
Olivia, to ask the court to assess the mother and her complete family including
her parents and brother.

[
30
]

Accordingly, this avenue was not further explored.  Then, in his
report dated October 27, 2008, Dr. Weinberger made essentially the same
recommendation as the mother had proposed over 1.5 years earlier.  He stated:

Olivia is caught between the parents she loves
and their ongoing conflict and she is beginning to show signs of strain.  She
will benefit from seeing a counsellor to afford her with private opportunity to
sort through her feelings given the sensitivities and difficulties between the
parents and how she can find herself exposed to it.  In addition, the counsellor
could be asked regularly or periodically to help determine Olivia’s preferences
as to activities or the like when parents may themselves be unclear or are in
conflict as to her true wishes.

[
31
]

The mother pursued the recommendation with Olivia’s family doctor in
November 2008.  On the same day, she e-mailed the father that this doctor also
thought Olivia would benefit strongly from seeing a professional therapist to
talk about her feelings regarding ongoing family matters.  He had recommended a
Dr. Martin.  Mr. Greenberg replied promptly:  he did not consent to this
doctor.  The next day, on November 26, 2008, he wrote directly to the family
doctor, as follows:

I would like to inform you that I am Olivia
Greenberg’s father.  Apparently, my ex wife, Manya Greenberg and my daughter,
Olivia came to visit you yesterday for Olivia’s annual checkup and to have her
stomach aches assessed.  Please be advised that I have legal joint custody of
Olivia and I am fully entitled to receive ALL information or recommendations
that you may provide to my ex wife regarding my daughter.

As per the email Manya Greenberg sent to me on
today’s date, please confirm in writing the recommendations you allegedly
stated to her, the information you received to justify said recommendations,
and what did
Olivia
and
Manya Greenberg
say to you
to justify your recommendations and conclusion as per Manya Greenberg’s
statement in her email.  This is not “privacy issue” as Olivia is my daughter.
Please find an excerpt from Manya Greenberg’s email:

“He (Dr. Esdaile) said that she would benefit
strongly by seeing a professional therapist to talk about her feelings
regarding our ongoing family matters.  He believed it would help her out a lot
as her stomach problems are likely due to stress”

Dr. Esdaile, given the seriousness of said
matter, I do not want to automatically accept my ex wife’s statements at face
value, so I would appreciate if you could be so kind to confirm (in writing)
precisely the information conveyed to you by Manya Greenberg and Olivia to
justify your recommendations/conclusions and the statements and recommendations
you made to my ex-wife regarding Olivia.  As time is of the essence, I am
hopeful that you may respond as soon as possible.

[
32
]

Dr. Esdaile replied the very next day, confirming his advice and
recommendation to Ms. Greenberg.  Mr. Greenberg still did not accept the
referral to Dr. Martin.  When asked about this in cross-examination, he stated in
effect:  Who is Dr. Esdaile?  He is just a GP.  Ms. Greenberg obtained two
other names from Dr. Esdaile.  Both were rejected by Mr. Greenberg.  Finally,
in March 2009, agreement was reached to send Olivia to confidential counselling
with Dr. Korneluk.  More than two years had passed since the mother first
requested the father’s consent to this.

[
33
]

Subsequently, despite the parents’ acknowledged agreement that this
was to be private counselling for Olivia, not to involve the parents nor to be
used for court purposes, Mr. Greenberg copied two letters to her in the summer
of 2009.  Both letters were written to the mother’s lawyer.  Both are four
pages long, strongly critical of the mother.  In the first letter, he described
her behaviour of standing talking to Sarah’s father, while both waited for him
to return Olivia and Sarah to his house for pick up, as “horrible and
shameful”, “outright malicious behaviour and harassment”.  In the second
letter, he said that the mother and her parents were ruining Olivia’s life.  He
quoted an e-mail ostensibly written by Olivia, emphasizing Olivia’s views and
preferences.  Olivia has stated that her father helped her write this e-mail,
and I have found that he did so and that it reflects his influence upon her.
In this letter, he also states what Dr. Korneluk believes, yet, assuming his
statement to be accurate, I question how would he know this if he had respected
the parents’ agreement that this was private counselling only for Olivia.

[
34
]

At the opening of trial, Mr. Greenberg announced his intention to
call Dr. Korneluk as a witness, despite his prior agreement not to.
Subsequently, he abandoned this plan.

•

Flu Shot

[
35
]

In November 2007, Ms. Greenberg happened to telephone Olivia at a
time when she was in her father’s car en route to having a flu shot.  This was
the first Ms. Greenberg had heard of it.  She e-mailed Mr. Greenberg reminding
him that she was responsible for Olivia’s health needs and of how harmful it
could have been for Olivia to receive this shot without notice to her, in case
Olivia had already had it.

[
36
]

Mr. Greenberg responded by saying, “Please stop your incessant lying
that you were not given advance notice.”  Of course, this had not been the
mother’s complaint; it was the coincidental timing of the notice and that it
came from Olivia, not from her father in a more timely way, that concerned Ms.
Greenberg.  Equally troubling is Mr. Greenberg’s remark that, “If you don’t
believe Louise or me, Olivia will verify the facts.”

•

Conclusion on Medical Issues

[
37
]

Provision of dental care and recent flu and meningitis shots for
Olivia do show that some parental cooperation has occurred on health related
issues.  But, the events described above satisfy me that overall the joint decision
making on major medical issues has created significant conflict and has exposed
Olivia to harm.  Her father has exposed her to the use of a drug, Ventolin,
contraindicated by the child’s specialist.  Her father denied her counselling
that she could have benefited from, for over two years.  Her father has exposed
her to receiving two flu shots in the same season by his failure to contact the
mother directly on this matter.  Mr. Greenberg has shown a disregard for the
opinions of medical professionals who had been treating Olivia on a long
standing basis, in preference to his own judgment on the issue.  Olivia almost
lost her allergist by reason of her father’s conduct towards him.  Effective
co-parenting on medical issues is not probable when one parent clearly lacks
respect for the medical professionals involved in the care of his daughter.

School Related Issues

•

After School Care

[
38
]

In January 2007, Mr. Greenberg made an anonymous
call to the Children’s Aid Society (the “Society”) reporting Ms. Greenberg for
leaving Olivia unsupervised after school.  In the result, both mother and
daughter were interviewed by a Society social worker.  The facts were that on
Wednesdays, Ms. Greenberg knew she would routinely be 15 minutes or so late in
picking Olivia up from school.  She directed Olivia to walk the several steps
between Hillel Academy and the Jewish Community Centre (“JCC”) and to wait for
her mother there.  It was not disputed that the two buildings are close by each
other and that a number of students in Olivia’s age group adopted the same
practice.  Despite acknowledging these facts, Mr. Greenberg described this as
an emergency and as irresponsible conduct by the mother warranting a call to
the Children’s Aid Society.  Not only did Mr. Greenberg expose his daughter to
a Children’s Aid Society interview, he also involved her in the dispute, and at
the same time as acknowledging how he had done so, stated that he had not.  Mr.
Greenberg wrote the following e-mail to Ms. Greenberg.

For the record I didn’t involve Olivia.  I
simply asked Olivia what she does after school and she mentioned this to me and
Louise.  Louise and I were shocked to say the least.  I told Olivia this was
not right and that I would send her mother an email to discuss the matter.  End
of story.  Olivia was not involved in any way.

[
39
]

This is one example of a disturbing observation
I made with respect to Mr. Greenberg.  He says something believing it to be
true and accurate, when on the face of it, the reality is different.  In this
example, he clearly involved Olivia, by asking her, as well as by telling her
it was wrong and that he would correct her mother.  Yet, in his mind, Olivia
was not involved in any way.  Both Justice Parfett, who ordered the assessment,
and Dr. Weinberger referred to this complaint by the father as indicative of
the high conflict in the case.  When asked whether he agreed, the father said,
“I must be missing something here…I’m scratching my head.”  It is troubling
that what is apparent to neutral third parties is elusive to Mr. Greenberg.

[
40
]

This conflict impacted negatively upon Olivia.
Absent her father’s agreement to her waiting at the JCC, she waited for her
mother on Wednesdays in the principal’s office.

•

Hebrew Tutoring

[
41
]

Conflict also arose over in class Hebrew
tutoring for Olivia.  Her teacher called Ms. Greenberg to suggest that Olivia
would benefit from some in class Hebrew tutoring.  Ms. Greenberg agreed, and
notified Mr. Greenberg right away.  Although he agreed to the extra help, he
attacked the teacher’s credibility in a letter to the school that also threatened
litigation, this because the teacher had only spoken to Ms. Greenberg.

I would like to formerly advise you that I have
legal joint custody of my daughter Olivia Greenberg and my ex-wife must gain my
consent on all education matters at your school.  Despite the fact I agree with
this tutoring decision, your school MUST contact me prior to any decisions made
and your school MUST gain my consent for all education issues that affect my
daughter.

If you have an issue or problem with my request
and instruction, please advise immediately as I will take the necessary legal
steps to enforce my legal and implied rights as Olivia’s father.

High School

[
42
]

The final Order dated July 22, 2005 provides
that the mother has principal residence of the child for school boundary
purposes.  Given that Olivia was already enrolled at Hillel Academy, this
clause would come into play if her grandparents were no longer willing or able
to fund her schooling there, which is not suggested, or when she is ready to
enter high school.  This will occur in two years, after Olivia graduates grade
8.

[
43
]

Mr. Greenberg has applied to change that
provision so that he would have primary residence for school boundary
purposes.  He would like to see Olivia attend high school in his neighbourhood,
which is in the same end of town as Hillel Academy.

[
44
]

For her part, the mother has recently moved and
one factor in her choice of location was the available high schools for Olivia
to choose between.  Future disagreement over which high school Olivia will
attend is likely.

•

School Uniforms

[
45
]

There was also a disagreement this year with
respect to payment for Olivia’s school uniforms.  This is the first year Hillel
Academy required uniforms.  The mother made $650 worth of purchases.  The
father’s objections were that the school had estimated the average cost per
pupil at $325, the mother had purchased two of every item, and since she was
purchasing school attire, she would not need to purchase so many regular
clothes for Olivia.  He called this a “wash” and deferred any contribution
pending this court’s ruling on the issue.

•

Conclusion on School Related Issues

[
46
]

Despite the primary agreement between the
parents for Olivia to attend Hillel Academy, the fact that they have
successfully exchanged details about Olivia’s schooling and homework and the
fact that both agree for future French tutoring for her, there has been
conflict between them on school related issues and future disagreement is
foreseeable with respect to Olivia’s high school.

Olivia’s Extracurricular Activities

[
47
]

The July 22, 2005 final Order dealt with
extracurricular activities as follows:

The parties will keep each other [informed]
about Olivia’s recreational and extracurricular activities and both parties
shall be entitled to attend any of Olivia’s activities irrespective of the
access schedule.

The Law

The
Divorce Act

[
146
]

Subsection 16(1)
of the
Divorce
Act,
R.S., 1985, c. 3 (2nd Supp.) provides that a court may make an order
respecting custody of and/or access to children of the marriage.
Subsection
16(6)
further provides that the court may make an order for a definite or
indefinite period or until the happening of a specified event and may impose
such other terms, conditions or restrictions in connection therewith as it
thinks fit and just.

[
147
]

Subsections 17(1)
and
(2)
of
the
Divorce Act
provide that a court may vary a custody order, or any
provision thereof, on the application of either former spouse. According to
subsection 17(3), a variation order may include any provision that, under the
Act, could have been included in the original order. However, subsection 17(5)
stipulates that before the court varies a custody order, it must be satisfied
that there has been a change in the condition, means, needs or other
circumstances of the child since the original order was made.

[
148
]

Subsection 17(5) also states
that the court may only vary a custody order if it is in the best interests of
the child to do so, as determined by reference to the condition, means, needs
and other circumstances of the child. As is the case with any custody order,
subsection 17(6) stipulates that the past conduct of a party will only be
relevant where it relates to his or her ability to act as a parent to the child. Finally, subsection 17(9) states that the court must
respect the principle that children should have as much contact with each
parent as is consistent with their best interests.

The Case Law

Material Change in Circumstances

[
149
]

In
Gordon v. Goertz
,
1996 CanLII 191 (SCC)
, [1996]
2 S.C.R. 27 at paras.
10-11
, the Supreme Court confirmed that the court must
find that there has been a material change in the circumstances of the child
before it can consider varying a custody order. The
purpose of this requirement is so that “an application to vary custody cannot
serve as an indirect route of appeal from the original custody order.”

[
150
]

The Supreme Court stated at para. 13 in
Gordon v. Goertz
that for a
change in circumstances to be considered a
material change
, the
following three criteria must be shown to exist:

(1)        a change in the condition, means, needs or circumstances
of the child and/or the ability of the parents to meet the needs of the child;

(2)        which materially affects the child; and

(3)        which
was either not foreseen or could not have been reasonably contemplated by the
judge who made the initial order.

[
151
]

The Ontario Court of Appeal,
in
Montgomery v. Montgomery
(1992),
1992 CanLII 8642 (ON CA)
, [1993] 97 D.L.R. (4th) 437 at
458-62, held that what may have appeared to be in a child’s best interests at
the time of a court order may no longer meet the needs of that child at a later
point in her development. The court noted that the requirement of a material
change is necessary in order to protect children from “unnecessary and trivial
adversarial weaponry”. However, in this case it held that cumulative
unrelenting stress to the child and one parent caused by ongoing access visits
with the other parent was enough to justify a variation order. The intensity of
the stress itself constituted a material change from the circumstances that
were before the court when the original order was made.

Best Interests of the Child

[
152
]

In
Gordon v. Goertz
,
supra

at paras.
17-25
, the Supreme Court of Canada stated that once a material change
in circumstances has been established, the court should consider the matter
anew with regard to the present circumstances instead
of defaulting to the existing arrangement. The inquiry cannot be limited to the
material change, as all factors bearing on the child’s best interests should be
considered. Ultimately, the “only issue when it comes to custody and access is
the welfare of the child whose future is at stake.”

[
153
]

The Supreme Court noted
that, in enacting the
Divorce Act
, Parliament provided two specific
directions as to the best interests of children. First of all, the conduct of
parents, “however meritorious or however reprehensible,” should only be
considered if it affects the ability of the parents to meet the child’s needs.
Secondly, the child should have as much contact with each parent as is
consistent with her best interests. According to the Supreme Court, this principle
is “mandatory, but not absolute.” A judge “can and should restrict access” if
he or she finds that the current custody and access schedule is not in the
child’s best interests.

[
154
]

In
Montgomery
,
supra
,
the Ontario Court of Appeal acknowledged that the needs of children are
inextricably tied to those of their parents, and the economic and emotional
needs of parents must therefore be factored into the
consideration of a child’s best interests. However, the court held that “the
central figure in the assessment is the dependent child.” That is why the
existence of a parental relationship does not guarantee parental rights to
custody or access. Rather, the “rights in custody and access are those of the
child.” While the court noted that this consideration will ideally lead to an
ongoing positive relationship with both parents, it found that the judge in
this case had not erred in determining that it was in the best interests of the
child to discontinue access visits with one parent.

High Conflict and Joint Custody

[
155
]

In some cases, the Ontario
Court of Appeal has held joint custody to be appropriate, even where there is a
history of repeated intense conflict between the parties. For example, in
Ladisa
v. Ladisa
(2005),
2005 CanLII 1627 (ON CA)
, 11 R.F.L. (6th) 50 at paras.
12-16
, the court upheld a
joint custody order where the trial judge had found that the children were in
need of “the parenting that both parents could give them.” She had been
satisfied that, despite the conflict between them, in situations such as
emergencies or where the parents were forced to be together in public, they had
shown that they were capable of putting the children’s interests ahead of their
own and communicating effectively.

[
156
]

However, in
Kaplanis v.
Kaplanis
(2005),
2005 CanLII 1625 (ON CA)
, 249 D.L.R. (4th) 620 at paras.
2
, 11-14, a decision
released the same day as
Ladisa, supra
, the Court of Appeal held that
joint custody was not appropriate where there was no effective cooperation
between the parents. The court set aside an order for joint custody because
there was no evidence that the parents were able to put aside their differences
and communicate effectively. The court held that one parent professing an
inability to communicate with the other parent will not, in and of itself,
preclude a joint custody order. On the other hand, joint custody orders cannot
be made with the expectation that communication between the parties will
improve after the litigation is over. At the time an order is made, there must
be some evidence of historical cooperation and appropriate communication between
the parties. No matter how detailed the custody order, the evolving needs of
the child and unexpected situations will have to be dealt with on an ongoing
basis. In order for joint custody to be feasible, the parties must, at the very
least, be able to agree on a process for resolving their differences.

[
157
]

The Court of Appeal
reiterated in
Roy v. Roy
(2006),
2006 CanLII 15619 (ON CA)
, 27 R.F.L. (6th) 44 at paras.
1-11
and
in
Lawson v. Lawson
(2006),
2006 CanLII 26573 (ON CA)
, 81 O.R. (3d) 321 at paras.
14-27
, that while
one parent cannot deliberately create problems and then claim sole custody,
joint or parallel custody will not be appropriate where there is a genuine
inability to effectively cooperate and communicate. In
Roy v. Roy
the
Court of Appeal noted that virtually the entire record “established that a
foundation for a joint or parallel custody order had been and continued to be
entirely missing.” In
Lawson v. Lawson
, it held that the trial judge was
in the best position to evaluate the behaviour of the parties and to decide
whether there was a genuine inability to co-parent. The trial judge had based
his order on a report by the Office of the Children’s Lawyer which found that
access visits were causing the children to suffer from stress and tension.

Stress to the Child

[
158
]

The courts have continually
found that joint custody is not appropriate where conflict between the parents
has caused visible signs of stress to the child. For example, in
Smith v.
Brandenburg
,

[1991] O.J. No. 1628
(Ct. J. (Prov. Div.)), the judge found that it was
necessary to alter a joint custody arrangement by awarding sole custody to one
of the parents. In that case, the parents described many events where they had
had heated disagreements, including several instances of conflict relating to
the child’s extracurricular activities and minor changes to the access
schedule. Their lack of ability to communicate directly would often lead to an
exchange of lawyer’s letters. The child had become more aware of the conflict
between her parents as she became older, and this had placed an increasing
amount of stress on her as she was often in a position where she had to choose
one loved parent over the other.

[
159
]

The stressful effects of
continuing conflict on the child were also a central consideration in
Montgomery
v. Montgomery
,
supra
. In that case, the Court of Appeal upheld the
trial judge’s finding that while the parent whose access was to be discontinued
had not emotionally abused the child, “his obsession with maintaining contact
with his daughter at all costs” and his conduct in relation to the mother had
caused a great deal of stress for his daughter.

[
160
]

Finally, in
Wreggitt v.
Belanger
(2001),
2001 CanLII 20827 (ON CA)
, 23 R.F.L. (5th) 457 at paras.
12
, 18-20, the trial judge
changed a joint custody arrangement by awarding sole custody to one parent
after finding that worsening conflict between the parents amounted to a
material change in circumstances. She made the following remarks in her
decision:

The children’s well-being ... is being detrimentally affected by the
current form of custody and the current schedule, and the children’s behaviour
has deteriorated. The manner in which the father has pursued this litigation
has impacted the children both directly and indirectly. The father’s view is
that the mother continues to try to “keep him from his children”. The father's
view in this regard is I find completely unfounded. The father[’s] approach to
joint parenting with the mother exhibits disdain towards her as a joint
custodial parent. The children are under a tremendous amount of stress. The
father’s pursuit of [an] “equal number of days” has been a direct contributor
to this stress. I also have some serious concerns as to how the children’s
emotional needs are being met while they are in the care of their father and
[his second wife].

[
161
]

The Ontario Court of Appeal
upheld the variation order, stating that “there was ample evidence to support
the trial judge’s finding of ‘worsening conflict between the parties’.” The
court remarked that “[c]onflict and lack of co-operation, whatever the source,
are an impediment to an effective joint parenting arrangement, as well as a
source of stress for the children…. Any cause for optimism [at the time of the
initial order] that the parties could overcome their hostility and co-parent
effectively, had clearly vanished [by the time of the variation order]”.

Application of the Law to this Case

[
162
]

The first issue is whether
there has been a material change of circumstances since the final Order dated
July 22, 2005 with respect to joint decision making or with respect to the
living arrangements for Olivia.  I am satisfied that there has been a material
change in circumstances warranting a change from joint decision making to sole
decision making.  Since the final Order was made, the parents have not
established an effective co-parenting regime.  They have had many serious
disagreements related to Olivia’s medical care, counselling, and recreational
activities, which have impacted in negative ways upon Olivia.  They have been
unable to successfully interpret the final Order in a consensual way with
respect to holidays, the weekend rotation following holidays, Mother’s Day, and
summer camp.  The parents have been unable to bring flexibility to the
parenting relationship in a successful way.  Acrimony has flared up when they
have been together in Olivia’s presence causing observable distress to her.  A
number of the good faith provisions in the final Order have been breached.
Olivia has been involved in their conflict and impacted by it.  She has been
drawn into their disputes and into the litigation and this has had a serious
negative impact upon her, causing her to see her father as a victim and her
mother as their adversary.  Olivia’s great need has been described by Dr.
Weinberger as a resolution that will bring the conflict to an end.

[
163
]

In my view, the joint
decision making prescribed in the final Order has proved unworkable.  Joint
parental decision making has been shown not to be in Olivia’s best interest,
rather to the contrary.  The conflict resolution clause set out in the final
Order has not worked successfully.  The parties were unable to agree to utilize
any of the processes set out in it, with the result being the commencement of
this litigation.  This breakdown of the joint decision making and conflict
resolution process could not reasonably have been contemplated or foreseen when
the Order was made.  In addition, what may have appeared to be in Olivia’s best
interests at that time has been shown not to be meeting her needs at this time,
because of the conflict she has been exposed to and the stress she is under
because of it.  Whatever reasons the parties had in 2005 to believe that they
could overcome their hostility and co-parent effectively have long since vanished,
to paraphrase the Court of Appeal in
Wreggitt v. Belanger
, supra
.  These
parents do not even agree now on a process for resolving their differences.

[
164
]

Accordingly, I find that
there has been a material change in circumstances warranting a variation of the
joint custody order to one of sole custody to the mother.  She is the parent
who has contributed less to the conflict, who has drawn Olivia into the
conflict and litigation less and who is better able, as between the parents, to
maintain an even keel and to self monitor.  Her anger with the father is
significantly less intense than his with her.  For these reasons, she is better
suited to be the sole custodial parent for Olivia because she is less likely to
use this authority to try to marginalize the father from Olivia’s life.  And,
the mother is the only parent who sought sole custody at trial.

[
165
]

The final Order dated July
22, 2005 put Mr. Greenberg in charge of Olivia’s dental care.  He chose Dr.
Landau as her dentist and, more recently, chose an orthodontist to consult with
about Olivia’s potential future orthodontic needs.  Olivia’s dental care has
not caused any issues between the parents until recently when Mr. Greenberg
took her to the dentist his wife works for, in lieu of Dr. Landau, because an
early appointment was available.  Ms. Greenberg appeared concerned about this.
Provided Dr. Landau remains Olivia’s dentist for all purposes, I see no reason
why Mr. Greenberg cannot continue in charge of her dental care.

[
166
]

With respect to the living
arrangements, I do not find that the father’s remarriage and the presence of a
stepdaughter in his home constitute a material change in circumstances.  I do
not regard these as factors that were unforeseeable in July 2005, or beyond

[
167
]

Mr. Greenberg also relies on
Olivia’s views and preferences as constituting a material change in
circumstances.  Olivia will be 11 years old in December 2009.  Dr. Weinberger
testified that her views were partly due to influence and partly her own.  I am

with one parent against the other is not in Olivia’s best interest.

[
168
]

I also want to comment on
something that Ms. Greenberg said in testimony that was repeated by her counsel

Greenberg’s access to Olivia reduced despite her concerns that he was

about the impact of negative influence from her father on Olivia.  This is an

The Custody and Access Order

[
169
]

The history of ineffective
co-parenting and Olivia’s need for a resolution that will bring parental
conflict to an end speak to the need for an order that is clear, certain, and
not open to discussion or debate between the parents.  The provision of sole
custody to Ms. Greenberg is intended to eliminate the parental conflict which
occurred when joint decision making was attempted.  It is not intended to
enable her to override Mr. Greenberg’s access time with Olivia or to determine
the access schedule.  Rather, the schedule must be clear and nonvariable in
order to meet the objective of conflict-free stability and consistency for
Olivia.  To this end, I have provided for sole custody to Ms. Greenberg, with
some limitations, as to Olivia’s dentist, Jewish faith, and place of
residence.  I have set out an exact schedule by which Olivia shall reside with
each parent and have removed from it the ability for either parent to request
changes, extensions, or special occasions, which were fraught with difficulty
under the prior Order.  I have defined each holiday and provided exactly how
the weekend rotation will pick up at the end of each.  With respect to
extracurricular activities, each parent may enroll Olivia in activities only on
that parent’s exclusive days, without the consent or agreement of the other
parent.  Only the parent who enrolled Olivia in the activity may attend any
special recitals or performances in respect of that activity.

[
170
]

It is my view that this
order, inflexible and set in stone as it is, is the type of order most probable
to reduce the parental conflict and Olivia’s exposure to it.  I hope that what
she loses in terms of occasional flexibility and common weekend activities will
be more than made up for by a significant reduction in the conflict to which
she is exposed.

[
171
]

The counselling recommended
by Dr. Weinberger should be undertaken by both parents and by Olivia.  This is
essential for each family member, for different reasons.  Ms. Greenberg should
continue to see Dr. Leonoff and should seek specific advice on helping Olivia
accept the outcome of this case and herself in improving her handling of
Olivia’s relationship with her father and stepmother.  Olivia should continue
to see Dr. Korneluk on a confidential basis so that she can discuss the outcome
with her in privacy and be assisted in acceptance of it, as well as other
issues as directed by Olivia herself.

[
172
]

Mr. Greenberg needs counselling,
as stated by Dr. Weinberger, to learn how to self calm, and how to interact and
correspond with the mother appropriately.  In addition, in my view, he requires
counselling to improve his ability to avoid parental conflict, to shield his
child from it, and to learn the importance for Olivia of his supporting her
relationship with her mother, including by refraining from making negative
remarks in Olivia’s presence.

[
173
]

In view of the importance of
this counselling to a successful outcome for Olivia, I make it a term and
condition to the mother’s custody and to the father’s access that this counselling
be undertaken and pursued.

[
174
]

mother and the father to a counsellor of their choosing to do the following:
